title: Musk Vows AI-Generated Odyssey Film by Year-End After Months of Attacking Nolan's Casting
excerpt: The Tesla CEO said his Grok Imagine platform would produce a 'historically accurate' full-length adaptation of Homer's epic, escalating a months-long feud with Christopher Nolan over the director's blockbuster version now past $280 million worldwide.
body:
• Elon Musk announced on X that Grok Imagine will produce a full-length, "historically accurate" Odyssey film before the end of 2026, reposting a three-minute AI-generated clip of scenes from Homer's epic.
  • The pledge deepens a months-long campaign against Christopher Nolan's casting of Lupita Nyong'o as Helen of Troy and Elliot Page in a supporting role, which Musk has called "anti-White."
  • Nolan's The Odyssey has earned over $280 million globally since its opening weekend, making it one of the biggest films of 2026 and the director's highest-grossing debut.
  • Critics and users pushed back on Musk's "historically accurate" framing, noting that The Odyssey is a mythological poem featuring cyclopes and sea monsters, not a historical document.

Elon Musk on Wednesday said his AI platform Grok Imagine would create a full-length adaptation of Homer's The Odyssey by the end of the year — one that is "historically accurate and true to the art of Homer." The announcement, made on his social media platform X at roughly 3 a.m., came as Christopher Nolan's star-studded film version of the ancient Greek epic continued to dominate the global box office.

"Before this year ends, Grok Imagine will make a full-length movie of The Odyssey that is historically accurate and true to the art of Homer," Musk wrote, sharing a three-minute AI-generated clip by X user @heavypulp depicting Odysseus speaking to the nymph Calypso about his desire to return home. The creator also posted a step-by-step breakdown of how the scene was produced using Grok's image and video generation tools.

From Online Feud to AI Counterprogramming

The post is the latest salvo in a months-long campaign by Musk against Nolan's film. The Tesla CEO and world's richest man has attacked the director repeatedly over casting decisions — principally the choice of Lupita Nyong'o, the Oscar-winning star of Black Panther, to play Helen of Troy and her twin sister Clytemnestra.

In a July 6 post viewed 1.8 million times, Musk wrote: "Chris Nolan desecrated Homer and groveled on his knees just to meet the woke rules required to win an Oscar. What a worm." In May, he called Nolan "an anti-White racist." He also amplified complaints about actor Elliot Page's involvement in the film, though Page plays a supporting role as a young soldier named Sinon, not Achilles as some users had incorrectly assumed.

Hours before his Grok announcement, Musk had responded to a user suggesting he put up $100 million for Mel Gibson "to film an Odyssey adaptation with painstakingly historically accurate ships, armour, weapons, and casting, with all dialogue taken straight from the original poem and delivered in Homeric Greek." Musk replied: "I'm down."

A Box Office Behemoth

Musk's campaign has done little to dent the film's commercial performance. Nolan's The Odyssey, starring Matt Damon as Odysseus, Tom Holland as his son Telemachus, Anne Hathaway as Penelope, and Zendaya in a supporting role, pulled in more than $264 million at the global box office on its opening weekend, according to Comscore. It has since crossed $280 million worldwide, making it the third-largest opening in the United States in 2026 and the biggest debut of Nolan's career.

On Monday alone, The Odyssey earned $18.67 million domestically, edging out Toy Story 5 at $17.3 million and The Mandalorian & Grogu's Memorial Day Monday of $16.4 million.

'There Is a Cyclops'

Musk's "historically accurate" framing drew swift mockery online. Users pointed out that The Odyssey is a mythological poem — not a historical chronicle — populated by gods, a cyclops, a six-headed sea monster, and enchantresses who turn men into pigs.

"'Historically accurate.' There is a cyclops."

— X user, responding to Musk's post

Others questioned the broader premise of replacing human actors with AI-generated content. "No thanks. The people want real actors," one user wrote. "Use AI to help humanity, not entertain us."

Whoopi Goldberg previously took aim at Musk's casting criticisms on The View, noting that "Lupita is also considered one of the world's most beautiful women" and asking: "I'm not sure what you're trying to say. You don't have to actually go to the movie." Actor Alec Baldwin also publicly defended Nyong'o, posting her photo on Instagram with the caption: "Dear Elon… but she IS the most beautiful woman in the world."

What Grok Imagine Can Actually Do

Grok Imagine is xAI's generative image and video tool integrated into X. While it can produce short clips and AI-generated imagery, creating a coherent feature-length film — with sustained character consistency, narrative pacing, and production quality comparable to a $200-million-plus studio release — would represent a leap far beyond what any publicly available AI system has demonstrated.

The three-minute clip Musk shared, while polished by current AI standards, underscores the gap: a handful of dialogue-driven scenes is a far cry from a two-hour film. Industry observers remain skeptical that Grok Imagine or any competing AI video tool could deliver on Musk's timeline, though rapid advances in generative video technology have repeatedly surprised the field.

Looking Ahead

The exchange underscores a widening culture-war front between Silicon Valley's AI ambitions and Hollywood's creative establishment. For Nolan, the numbers speak clearly enough — The Odyssey is tracking to become one of the top-grossing films of 2026. For Musk, the pledge adds another item to a long list of public promises with uncertain delivery dates, from full self-driving capability to Mars colonization.

Whether Grok Imagine produces anything resembling a feature film by December remains to be seen. What is already clear is that the debate over who gets to tell ancient stories — and how — has moved from academic seminars to the feeds of billionaires.
